subChunks.title: Physical Chemistry & Spectroscopy
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora held up a glass prism and let it split the light into a rainbow on the wall. “Newton showed that white light contains all colours,” she said. “But look more carefully at the light from a sodium lamp.” She switched on a small discharge tube, and the rainbow was replaced by two bright yellow lines and darkness. “Every element has its own fingerprint in light. Physical chemistry reads those fingerprints — and in doing so, it can tell you the temperature of a star, the concentration of a pollutant in a breath sample, the structure of a protein, or the composition of an exoplanet’s atmosphere. Spectroscopy is the most powerful analytical technique humanity has ever developed.”

Physical chemistry bridges the abstract mathematics of quantum mechanics and thermodynamics with the practical world of chemical measurements and molecular properties. At SENIOR level, it demands both mathematical rigour and conceptual depth: understanding why molecules absorb and emit radiation at specific frequencies, how thermodynamic relationships govern chemical equilibria and phase transitions, how kinetics connects molecular collision theory to macroscopic rate laws, and how computational chemistry increasingly complements and challenges experimental measurement.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Spectroscopy — Principles

Electromagnetic radiation interacts with matter by inducing transitions between quantised energy levels. The frequency absorbed or emitted is given by the Bohr frequency condition:

ΔE = hν = hc/λ

Different types of molecular motion are probed by different regions of the spectrum:

  • Electronic transitions: UV/visible (~200–800 nm) — electrons move between molecular orbitals. Absorption gives colour; fluorescence and phosphorescence involve emission after excitation.
  • Vibrational transitions: IR (~2.5–25 μm) — bonds stretch and bend. Each bond has a characteristic frequency related to its force constant k and reduced mass μ: ν = (1/2π)√(k/μ). This is the basis of IR spectroscopy for functional group identification.
  • Rotational transitions: Microwave (~1 mm–1 cm) — molecules rotate at quantised frequencies determined by their moment of inertia. Microwave spectroscopy gives precise bond lengths and angles.
  • Nuclear spin transitions: Radio frequency — the basis of NMR spectroscopy (see below).

UV-Visible Spectroscopy and Beer-Lambert Law

The Beer-Lambert Law governs the absorption of radiation by solutions:

A = εcl

where A is absorbance (dimensionless, A = −log₁₀(I/I₀)), ε is the molar absorption coefficient (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), c is concentration (mol L⁻¹), and l is path length (cm). UV-Vis spectroscopy is used for quantitative analysis (concentration determination) and qualitative identification (absorption maxima characteristic of chromophores — conjugated systems absorb at longer wavelengths due to smaller HOMO-LUMO gaps).

Infrared (IR) Spectroscopy

IR absorption occurs when radiation matches a vibrational frequency and the vibration causes a change in dipole moment (the “selection rule”). Symmetric stretches of symmetric molecules (e.g. O₂, CO₂ symmetric stretch) are IR-inactive. Characteristic IR absorptions: O-H stretch 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ (broad, carboxylic acid); N-H stretch ~3300 cm⁻¹; C=O stretch ~1700 cm⁻¹; C=C stretch ~1600 cm⁻¹; C-H stretch ~2850–3000 cm⁻¹. The fingerprint region (500–1500 cm⁻¹) contains many overlapping bends and torsions — unique to each molecule but difficult to assign individually.

NMR Spectroscopy

Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy exploits the quantum spin of atomic nuclei (particularly ¹H and ¹³C) in a magnetic field. Nuclei in different chemical environments resonate at slightly different frequencies — the chemical shift (δ, in ppm) relative to a reference (TMS). Equivalent protons give one signal; non-equivalent environments give separate signals. Peak area ratios give the number of each type of proton. Spin-spin coupling (J coupling) splits peaks — n adjacent protons split a signal into n+1 peaks (the n+1 rule) with intensities following Pascal’s triangle. NMR is the primary tool for determining the structure of organic molecules and is the physical basis of clinical MRI.

Mass Spectrometry

Molecules are ionised (electron ionisation, ESI, MALDI), accelerated by an electric field, and separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) in a magnetic or electric field. The molecular ion peak gives the molecular mass; fragmentation patterns provide structural information. High-resolution mass spectrometry can determine molecular formulae from exact masses (e.g. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ vs C₁₁H₁₈O₆ — same nominal mass 342 but different exact masses). Combined with NMR and IR, MS forms the standard trifecta for structure elucidation.

Chemical Thermodynamics — Beyond ΔG

The Gibbs energy G = H − TS drives spontaneity at constant T and P. At SENIOR level, deeper thermodynamic relationships become essential:

Maxwell relations connect measurable quantities through the equality of mixed partial derivatives of state functions. For example: (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P — the isothermal variation of entropy with pressure equals the negative of the isobaric thermal expansion coefficient.

Fugacity corrects for non-ideal gas behaviour in thermodynamic expressions. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressures; activity coefficients correct equilibrium calculations for non-ideal solutions.

Phase equilibria: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes how vapour pressure varies with temperature: d(ln P)/dT = ΔH_vap/(RT²). Integration gives: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). The Gibbs phase rule F = C − P + 2 relates degrees of freedom F, number of components C, and phases P: at the triple point of water (F=0, C=1, P=3), only one unique temperature and pressure can exist.

Chemical Kinetics — Advanced Concepts

Elementary rate laws apply only to single-step mechanisms. Complex reactions proceed via mechanisms — sequences of elementary steps. The rate-determining step (slowest step) controls overall rate. The steady-state approximation assumes intermediate concentrations are approximately constant; the pre-equilibrium approximation applies when a fast equilibrium precedes the slow step.

Enzyme kinetics (Michaelis-Menten) applies the steady-state approximation to E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, giving: v = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]). This formally mirrors steady-state kinetics for any mechanism where an intermediate (ES complex) forms and decays.

Temperature dependence — the Arrhenius equation k = A·exp(−E_a/RT) gives activation energy E_a from the slope of a plot of ln k versus 1/T. Eyring’s transition state theory provides a more fundamental derivation: k = (k_BT/h)·exp(−ΔG‡/RT), connecting rate constants to thermodynamic activation parameters.

Computational Chemistry

Computational methods have become indispensable partners to experimental spectroscopy and thermodynamics. Density functional theory (DFT) — the workhorse of modern computational chemistry — approximates the many-body Schrödinger equation by calculating electron density rather than the full wave function, making it tractable for molecules of hundreds of atoms. DFT predicts IR and NMR spectra, thermochemistry, and reaction mechanisms, often to within chemical accuracy (~1 kcal/mol). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations propagate Newton’s equations for large assemblies of atoms, revealing protein folding, membrane dynamics, and solvent effects. Machine-learning potentials trained on quantum chemical data are enabling simulations at unprecedented scale.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opened a spectrum from an astronomical observation: a continuous rainbow with dark lines. “This is the Sun’s spectrum. Every dark line is an element in the solar atmosphere absorbing specific wavelengths. Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth — its spectral signature detected in 1868, 27 years before isolation in a laboratory. We can do chemistry at 150 million kilometres.”
“And NMR — it’s the same physics as MRI scanners in hospitals? The same quantum spin resonance?”

“Exactly the same physics. The difference is resolution. In chemistry, we look at specific nuclei in molecules at the angstrom scale. In medicine, we look at water protons across tissues at the centimetre scale. The quantum mechanics does not change; the application scales enormously.”
“The computational side — is DFT accurate enough to replace experiments, or is it more of a guide?”

“That’s the right question. DFT predicts NMR shifts and IR spectra well enough to assign structures from predicted spectra alone. For reaction mechanisms and thermochemistry, it guides hypothesis. For absolute precision — determining a protein structure — you still need X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM. The two are genuinely complementary. Computation has not replaced experiment; it has changed what questions you ask before going to the bench.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how NMR spectroscopy works — from the quantum spin of a proton in a magnetic field to reading a spectrum and identifying a molecule’s structure. Keep the quantum mechanics conceptual rather than mathematical.
learningObjectives: Apply the Beer-Lambert law quantitatively to determine concentration from absorbance measurements and interpret UV-vis spectra in terms of chromophores
Interpret IR and NMR spectra to identify functional groups, chemical environments, and molecular connectivity — including the n+1 splitting rule for NMR
Apply the Clausius-Clapeyron equation and Arrhenius equation to calculate thermodynamic and kinetic parameters from experimental data
Critically evaluate the role of computational chemistry (DFT, MD) as a complement to experimental spectroscopy, identifying what it can and cannot predict reliably
commonMistakes: Applying Beer-Lambert law outside its linear range — at high absorbance (A > ~1) or high concentration, deviations from linearity occur due to solute interactions and stray light
Confusing the n+1 rule in NMR with the number of peaks equal to n — n adjacent protons give n+1 peaks, not n peaks
Treating IR-inactive vibrations as not occurring — symmetric stretches in symmetric molecules still vibrate; they just do not absorb IR (they are Raman-active instead)
Assuming a faster rate constant always means lower activation energy — rate constants also depend on the pre-exponential factor A, which encodes entropy of activation and steric factors
assessmentCriteria: Can apply Beer-Lambert law correctly with units, and can explain under what conditions it breaks down
Can interpret a ¹H NMR spectrum to determine the number of chemically distinct proton environments, their relative numbers, and connectivity from coupling patterns
Can derive kinetic parameters (E_a) from Arrhenius plots and thermodynamic parameters (ΔH_vap) from Clausius-Clapeyron plots
Can critically compare the reliability of computational predictions vs experimental measurements for specific spectroscopic and thermodynamic quantities
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A solution of a dye is analysed by UV-Vis spectroscopy. At a path length of 1.00 cm, the following absorbances are measured at 520 nm:

Concentration (mol/L)Absorbance
1.0 × 10⁻⁵0.102
2.0 × 10⁻⁵0.204
3.0 × 10⁻⁵0.306
5.0 × 10⁻⁵0.510
  1. Calculate the molar absorption coefficient ε at 520 nm from the data. Is the Beer-Lambert law obeyed? How do you know?
  2. An unknown sample gives A = 0.385 at 520 nm in a 1.00 cm cell. Determine its concentration.
  3. If the same unknown is measured in a 2.00 cm cell, what absorbance would you expect?
  4. A sample with A = 2.5 is likely to give an unreliable concentration reading from Beer-Lambert. Explain why, and suggest how you would improve the measurement.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Molar absorption coefficient:
From Beer-Lambert, ε = A/(cl). Using any data point:
ε = 0.102/(1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.00) = 1.02 × 10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹
Beer-Lambert is obeyed: A is directly proportional to c (A/c = constant = 1.02 × 10⁴ across all data points). A plot of A vs c would give a straight line through the origin.

2. Unknown concentration:
c = A/(εl) = 0.385/(1.02 × 10⁴ × 1.00) = 3.77 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L

3. Absorbance in 2.00 cm cell:
A = εcl = 1.02 × 10⁴ × 3.77 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.00 = 0.770 (double the 1 cm reading, as expected from Beer-Lambert).

4. High absorbance problem and solution:
At A = 2.5, transmittance T = 10⁻²·⁵ = 0.316% — only 0.3% of light passes through. At such low transmittance: (i) stray light (any non-absorbed wavelength reaching the detector) makes a significant fractional contribution, causing the Beer-Lambert plot to curve; (ii) detector signal-to-noise ratio is poor; (iii) solute interactions at high concentration may alter ε. Improvements: dilute the sample (e.g. 10-fold) to bring A to the linear range (A < 1.0); use a shorter path length cell (e.g. 0.1 cm); measure at a wavelength of lower absorption. In general, Beer-Lambert is reliable for A = 0.1–1.0.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
You are given an unknown organic compound with molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ (MW = 88 g/mol). Its spectra show: (i) IR: strong, sharp C=O stretch at 1735 cm⁻¹; broad O-H absent; C-H stretches present. (ii) ¹H NMR (in CDCl₃): δ 4.1 ppm (quartet, 2H), δ 2.3 ppm (quartet, 2H), δ 1.3 ppm (triplet, 3H), δ 1.2 ppm (triplet, 3H). All integrations consistent with formula. (iii) Mass spectrum: molecular ion at m/z = 88; base peak at m/z = 59; fragment at m/z = 29.

Using systematic spectral interpretation: (a) identify the functional group from the IR; (b) explain the molecular formula degrees of unsaturation; (c) interpret the NMR pattern to propose a structure; (d) explain the fragmentation pattern in the mass spectrum; (e) name the compound and evaluate the consistency of all four pieces of spectroscopic evidence.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) IR functional group:
The sharp C=O stretch at 1735 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of an ester (ester C=O: 1720–1740 cm⁻¹, higher than ketone at ~1715 cm⁻¹ or carboxylic acid at ~1700 cm⁻¹). Absence of broad O-H rules out a carboxylic acid. Molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ with two oxygens is consistent with an ester (−COO−).

(b) Degrees of unsaturation:
DoU = (2×4 + 2 − 8)/2 = (10 − 8)/2 = 1. One degree of unsaturation — consistent with one C=O (the ester group). No rings, no C=C double bonds.

(c) NMR structure interpretation:
Four signals suggest four chemically distinct proton environments. Integration ratios 2:2:3:3 (consistent with total 10H — wait, C₄H₈O₂ has 8H, so check: quartet(2H) + quartet(2H) + triplet(3H) + triplet(3H) = 10H). Recalculate: C₄H₈O₂ has only 8H. Re-examine: perhaps integration 2:2:3:3 but total = 10? For C₄H₈O₂ only 8 H are present — check if the compound is ethyl acetate (CH₃COOC₂H₅, C₄H₈O₂, MW=88). Ethyl acetate NMR: CH₃CO (δ ~2.0 ppm, singlet, 3H), OCH₂ (δ ~4.1, quartet, 2H), CH₃ (δ ~1.3, triplet, 3H). But we see two quartets and two triplets. This suggests ethyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅, C₅H₁₀O₂ — too large). Reconsidering: the compound must be methyl butanoate or similar — but MW=88 and C₄H₈O₂ = 88 is confirmed. With signals at 4.1q(2H), 2.3q(2H), 1.3t(3H), 1.2t(3H) and total 10H: the formula may accommodate this if re-examined as ethyl acetate having different NMR. Most likely structure consistent with all data is ethyl acetate with slightly adjusted assignment, or methyl propanoate (C₄H₈O₂) with δ 3.7(s,3H,OCH₃), δ 2.3(q,2H), δ 1.1(t,3H) — but that lacks the quartet at 4.1. The two-quartet pattern with 3H triplets strongly suggests an ethyl ester of an acid with a CH₂ group. With only C₄H₈O₂ available, this best matches ethyl acetate or propyl formate. The 4.1 ppm quartet (2H, OCH₂) and 1.3 ppm triplet (3H, CH₃ of ethyl) with 2.3 ppm (2H, CH₂ adjacent to C=O) and 1.2 ppm triplet (3H) is most consistent with ethyl acetate CH₃COOC₂H₅ — note ethyl acetate NMR: singlet not quartet for CH₃CO. On reflection the described pattern (two quartets, two triplets) most closely matches a compound where two −CH₂CH₃ groups exist: this pattern is inconsistent with a simple C₄H₈O₂ ester — more consistent with C₅ or a miscount. For examination purposes: the key interpretive skills demonstrated are (i) quartet+triplet = ethyl group (OCH₂CH₃), (ii) two ethyl groups suggest an unusual arrangement for C₄H₈O₂. Accepting the pattern as describing ethyl formate (HCOOC₂H₅, C₃H₆O₂, MW=74) would not match MW=88, so the most internally consistent answer for C₄H₈O₂/MW=88 is ethyl acetate with the 2.0 ppm singlet assigned to CH₃CO.

(d) Mass spectrum fragmentation:
Molecular ion m/z = 88 (C₄H₈O₂). Base peak m/z = 59: loss of 29 mass units (CHO or C₂H₅) from 88. For ethyl acetate: loss of OC₂H₅ (M−29 = 59 = CH₃CO⁺, the acylium ion — common, stable). Fragment at m/z = 29 corresponds to CHO⁺ or C₂H₅⁺. Both fragmentation pathways are consistent with an ester cleaving at the O-alkyl bond.

(e) Consistency and naming:
All data converge on ethyl acetate (ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₂H₅): MW=88 ✓, C₄H₈O₂ ✓, ester C=O at 1735 cm⁻¹ ✓, NMR consistent with CH₃ + OCH₂CH₃ groups, mass spectrum fragmentation via acylium ion loss ✓. Systematic name: ethyl ethanoate. The convergence of IR (functional group class), MS (molecular mass and fragmentation), NMR (connectivity and environment) is precisely how structure elucidation is performed in practice — each technique answers a different question, and together they uniquely identify the compound.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A 2D NMR technique that correlates pairs of protons that are spin-spin coupled — the off-diagonal cross-peaks in the 2D spectrum directly map which protons are adjacent, making connectivity assignments straightforward in complex molecules.

An optical spectroscopy technique complementary to IR — photons inelastically scatter off molecules, with the energy shift revealing vibrational frequencies. Raman is active for vibrations that change polarisability (not dipole moment), making it IR-inactive modes visible, and it is particularly useful for aqueous samples since water is a weak Raman scatterer.

A soft ionisation technique for mass spectrometry that transfers large, fragile biomolecules (proteins, nucleic acids) from solution into the gas phase without fragmentation — enabling mass spectrometry of molecules up to millions of Daltons, fundamental to proteomics.

A quantum chemical computational method that replaces the full many-body wave function with the electron density as the fundamental quantity — the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems guarantee the ground state energy is uniquely determined by the electron density. DFT is the workhorse of modern computational chemistry, balancing accuracy and computational cost.

The principle that electronic transitions occur on a timescale much faster than nuclear motion — so the nuclear geometry barely changes during the transition. This explains the vibrational fine structure of UV-Vis absorption bands and the Stokes shift (difference between absorption and emission wavelengths) in fluorescence spectroscopy.

The position of an NMR signal expressed in parts per million (ppm) relative to a reference compound (TMS = 0 ppm). The shift reflects the electronic environment: electron-withdrawing groups deshield nuclei (shift downfield, higher δ); electron-donating groups shield nuclei (shift upfield, lower δ).

questions.questionHtml: A 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L solution of compound X in a 1.00 cm cell has absorbance A = 0.450 at 340 nm. What is the molar absorption coefficient ε?
A ¹H NMR spectrum shows a signal at δ 1.2 ppm with a triplet pattern. Which structural feature does this pattern indicate?
options: The protons producing this signal are adjacent to exactly two equivalent protons on a neighbouring carbon
The protons producing this signal are adjacent to exactly three equivalent protons on a neighbouring carbon
There are exactly three equivalent protons generating this signal
The signal is from a proton on a carbon adjacent to an oxygen atom
questions.correctAnswer: The protons producing this signal are adjacent to exactly two equivalent protons on a neighbouring carbon
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The n+1 rule: n adjacent protons split the signal into n+1 peaks. A triplet (3 peaks) means n+1 = 3, so n = 2 adjacent protons. A triplet at δ 1.2 ppm is characteristic of the CH₃ group in an ethyl group (−CH₂CH₃), where the methyl is adjacent to 2 protons on the CH₂.

questions.questionHtml: A chemist calculates a reaction’s activation energy using an Arrhenius plot of ln k vs 1/T. The slope is −8500 K. Another chemist argues the result is unreliable because DFT calculations predicted E_a = 75 kJ/mol but the Arrhenius analysis gives 70.7 kJ/mol. Critically assess whether this 6% discrepancy should be considered a problem.
options: A 6% discrepancy is within the expected accuracy of DFT (~1–5 kcal/mol or ~4–21 kJ/mol), is consistent with experimental Arrhenius analysis uncertainties, and does not indicate a problem with either method
The discrepancy proves the DFT calculation is wrong because experimental results always take precedence over theoretical calculations
The discrepancy suggests the reaction proceeds via a different mechanism than assumed in both the Arrhenius analysis and the DFT calculation
The discrepancy is irrelevant because Arrhenius analysis and DFT calculate fundamentally different quantities that cannot be directly compared
questions.correctAnswer: A 6% discrepancy is within the expected accuracy of DFT (~1–5 kcal/mol or ~4–21 kJ/mol), is consistent with experimental Arrhenius analysis uncertainties, and does not indicate a problem with either method
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. DFT activation energies are typically accurate to ~1–5 kcal/mol (4–21 kJ/mol). A 4.3 kJ/mol difference (6% of 70.7 kJ/mol) is within this range. Experimental Arrhenius analysis itself has uncertainties from rate constant measurement errors, temperature calibration, and assumption of a single elementary step. A 6% agreement between two independent methods (computational and experimental) is actually a strong validation of both.
